questions.title: How can a premium finance company cancel an insurance policy under a power of attorney?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the basic setup of this case. APAC wasn't the insurer; it was the company that financed the insureds' premiums. But the opinion says the finance agreements gave APAC a power of attorney allowing it to cancel the GoAuto policies if the insureds defaulted on their installment payments. Normally I think of cancellation as something the insurer does. Is APAC legally acting as the insured's agent when it sends the cancellation request, or is this some special statutory mechanism unique to premium finance arrangements? I'm trying to understand why Louisiana lets a third-party finance company trigger cancellation at all.

questions.title: Why did the court say "strict adherence" to the cancellation statute does not imply a signature requirement?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly says Louisiana requires strict adherence to the premium-finance cancellation statute and that any defect makes cancellation ineffective. But when the plaintiffs argued that "certifying" the statutory facts should require a signature before cancellation, the Fifth Circuit said strict adherence is not an invitation to add procedures the statute doesn't expressly contain. I'm struggling with that move. If Louisiana courts strictly construe this statute, how do courts decide whether something is a missing statutory requirement versus an impermissible extra-textual requirement? In other words, why wasn't a signature treated as part of what it means to "certify"?

questions.title: Does a notice "certify" statutory facts if it is unsigned and identifies no individual employee?
questions.question_body: Here, APAC's cancellation request said "APAC certifies that..." and then listed the required statutory statements, but no employee signed it until later in the morning, after GoAuto's system had already cancelled the policy. The notice also apparently didn't name any particular APAC employee. One Louisiana case the opinion cites, Benitez, mentioned that an unsigned document did not purport to certify anything. Is a company-level statement like "APAC certifies" enough by itself, or does certification usually imply some individual attestation? I'm not sure how corporate entities can 'certify' facts without a human signer.

questions.title: Can an insurer legally "receive" a cancellation request when only its computer system gets the message?
questions.question_body: The statute says the insurer may proceed to cancel the policy "upon receipt" of the notice and certification from the premium finance company. In this case, APAC's computer automatically sent an email/web-service request, GoAuto's computer system automatically processed it, and no person reviewed anything until later. The Fifth Circuit treated this as GoAuto having taken possession, delivery, or custody of the request. Is that a normal legal understanding of receipt in statutes like this? I'm especially confused because the plaintiffs argued the legislature used "receipt" rather than just "sending," which sounds like something more than a transmission hitting a server.

questions.title: When should a federal court certify an unresolved state-law question instead of making an Erie guess?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs asked the Fifth Circuit to certify the interpretation of terms like "certifying" and "receipt" to the Louisiana Supreme Court, and the panel refused. The opinion says the absence of a state supreme court decision is not enough by itself and that the Fifth Circuit is "chary" about certification absent a compelling reason. Under Erie, how do federal courts decide when to certify versus when to predict state law themselves? Since this issue apparently affects Louisiana's insurance industry and there wasn't controlling Louisiana Supreme Court authority, what more would have been needed to justify certification?

questions.title: How did deciding only the cancellation-procedure issue justify dismissing all claims with prejudice?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the parties filed summary judgment motions 'solely' on whether GoAuto's cancellation procedure complied with Louisiana law. But the complaint also alleged misrepresentations and breach of good faith and fair dealing. After finding no statutory violation, the district court dismissed all claims against GoAuto with prejudice, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed. Was every other claim necessarily derivative of the theory that the policies were never effectively cancelled? I'm trying to understand the procedural link between winning on the statutory-compliance issue and wiping out the entire case against GoAuto.

questions.title: Why could Nicholas Jenkins sue over the cancellation issue if he was not one of the financed insureds?
questions.question_body: Williams and Wright were former GoAuto insureds, but Jenkins is described as someone injured in an accident with a different GoAuto insured who had also financed that policy through APAC. Jenkins still became a plaintiff challenging whether that other driver's policy had been effectively cancelled. What gives Jenkins a cause of action here if he wasn't a party to the finance agreement or the policy? Is this because Louisiana allows a direct action against liability insurers, so an accident victim has an interest in whether the tortfeasor's insurance remained in force?
